title: Case: Shopify, the Modular Monolith That Serves Millions of Merchants
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/46-case-shopify/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (a thesis paragraph, a roadmap that announces every section, and a synthesis that answers the opening question); the three one-line 'Sources:' notes under the tables are folded into the paragraphs that introduce those tables, and the two opening paragraphs on dating the evidence are merged. These are recorded in decision_log.

know: Shopify's business with its own definitions (GMV, merchant, MRR): FY2025 revenue of $11.56 billion, about three quarters merchant solutions that the 10-K says are correlated with GMV; Shopify Payments carrying 65.6% of GMV and resold from licensed processors (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen) by Shopify entities that state they are not licensed as a payment institution; one multi-tenant, 'single branch' Rails platform.

The architecture record by date: the 2019 componentization, the 2020 state (2.8 million lines, 37 components, each depending on over half of the others), Packwerk kept as a gate on new base-layer dependencies, the February 2024 retrospective's admission that domains and boundaries 'do not reflect the way Shopify's code actually functions'; the Storefront Renderer carved out for measured latency behind a verifier; pods (2016–2018) and shop moves by shard balancing (2021), with the shop as sharding key and unit of isolation.

The landlord's cadence: checkout.liquid and Shopify Scripts withdrawn on published dates (announced February 2023; August 2024, August 2025, 30 June 2026), replaced by sandboxed extension points and Functions; webhooks at-least-once and unordered, retried 8 times over 4 hours and deleted after 8 consecutive failures, with reconciliation jobs expected of the consumer; API versions every three months, each supported for at least twelve months; rate limits per app per store; the agent interface (Storefront MCP, May 2025) replaced by UCP endpoints in 2026, with no EU buyer market on any agentic channel page read at the cut-off.

Peak figures with their definitions (BFCM 2025: $14.6 billion unaudited GMV, 489 million edge against 117 million app-server requests a minute) and where the evidence stops (today's topology, the checkout queue, merchant counts, Shop Pay claims, Sidekick's availability date).
believe: The useful Shopify for a merchant is the landlord's behavior, not the architecture: it changes the platform under everyone on dates it publishes.
Shopify's own record undermines the slogan made from it: it did not split its monolith into clean domains; it learned which gate was worth keeping.
can_do: List for their own platform which extension points and API versions their apps and connectors depend on, with support ends and owners.
Explain why a webhook-fed integration needs idempotent handling, a reconciliation job and a check that its subscription still exists.
Ask any SaaS vendor for its unit of isolation and whether it can move or restore one tenant alone.

audience.who: Newcomers to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or architect who hears 'Shopify kept a monolith' or 'just use Functions' in a review and needs the dated sources. Product managers and leaders whose brand rents a hosted shop platform are the second readers: for them the chapter describes the landlord's behavior (extension points withdrawn on dates, API windows, rate limits, agent channels switched on by default).
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

Kestrel & Pine, its people, its ten incidents in outline (among them the Black Friday Oversell and the Deprecated Endpoint) and the names of the sixteen failure patterns (among them the Giant's Boots, the Pulled Rug, the Secret Agent and the Forked Platform).

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product Kestrel & Pine rents and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system (OMS), availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II to X: available-to-promise; checkout creating the order once; authorization, capture, settlement and payout; app scopes, the app governance rule and the ownership map; API versioning and deprecation; peak planning; agent readiness (W8).

From the Part XI introduction: the four cases are read from dated sources researched on 7 November 2026, with documented, widely reported and inferred claims kept apart, and each case ends with what the evidence could not establish.
does_not_know: Shopify's reporting definitions: GMV (as Shopify defines it), merchant, MRR, Payments penetration, subscription and merchant solutions.
Multi-tenant, single branch, monolith, modular monolith, component, Packwerk, shard, sharding key, pod, Storefront Renderer.
Theme, Liquid, headless, Hydrogen, Oxygen, Storefront API, Lighthouse score; checkout extensibility, Shopify Functions, WebAssembly, Shop Pay, PCI DSS, payment orchestration.
Scope, OAuth, HMAC signature, rate limit, API version window; BFCM, CDN, edge and app-server requests; MCP, UCP, Catalog, agent profile, trust tier, Sidekick.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a silent integration failure after an outage, the reader explains it from the platform's documented webhook contract and names the merchant-side disciplines that prevent it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A merchant's stock-sync connector, fed by its hosted platform's webhooks, was down for five hours on a Friday night after its host failed. On Monday the stock on a marketplace is wrong and the connector logs no errors. Using only this chapter: what probably happened, and what should the merchant have had in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Shopify's documented contract: delivery is not guaranteed and not ordered; a failed delivery is retried 8 times over the next 4 hours, and after 8 consecutive failures the subscription is deleted automatically, so the connector stopped receiving events and had nothing to log. The merchant needs idempotent consumers that ignore duplicates by webhook id, a periodic reconciliation job that fetches state from the platform (Kestrel & Pine's W5), a check on the subscription itself, and every connector pinned to a dated API version with its support end and owner recorded.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader separates the Shopify practices a renting merchant should adopt from the machinery it should not copy, with the reason.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which Shopify practices should a merchant that rents a hosted platform adopt, which should it not, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Adopt: pinned API versions with their support ends as a maintenance budget for every connector; webhooks treated as at-least-once, unordered and reconciled; no checkout customization the platform could withdraw, custom behavior in the lowest sanctioned place; a boundary check in the build for any in-house code without chasing zero violations; shadow comparison with fallback before any cutover; load tests at forecast with caches bypassed and game days on the money paths, scaled down to connectors, ERP and WMS; asking vendors for their unit of isolation. Do not copy: pods, Ghostferry shard moves, a custom observability platform, a worldwide edge renderer, a readiness program that starts in March, which answer millions of shops. Reason: the platform changes under every merchant on published dates and the merchant's own failures were in the connectors, not the storefront.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can correct the slogan 'Shopify modularized its monolith' from the chapter's sources.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague says Shopify proves that a monolith can be split into clean domain modules without microservices. Using only this chapter: what does Shopify's record say?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Shopify kept one codebase as one deployment unit. It labeled about 6,000 classes by domain in 2019; in 2020 it had 2.8 million lines and 37 components, each depending on over half of the others. Packwerk stayed only as a gate against new base-layer dependencies, its privacy checks removed in version 3.0, and the February 2024 retrospective says domain boundaries do not reflect how the code functions, so components became organizational groupings. What paid off was ownership (a stewardship team per file, exceptions routed to owners) and one cheap gate; the one carve-out, the Storefront Renderer, was made for measured latency behind a verifier with fallback.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which work a hosted platform takes on and which the merchant's team still operates; Shopify's business figures (the FY2025 filing and the quarter to September 2026) kept apart from its architecture history (pods 2018, components 2019, shard balancing 2021, a 2024 retrospective), each account dated and not taken as today's design; the counterparts of a jacket order (product and stock, pages, checkout, payment, messages to the warehouse); revenue that follows sales with checkout as the protected path, the monolith kept and its boundary lessons, the shop as unit of isolation, and a platform that changes under everyone on published dates, including its agent interface; failure patterns The Giant's Boots, The Pulled Rug and The Secret Agent. Evidence: filings, engineering posts, developer documentation and changelogs, with inferences labeled.

thesis.question: What does Shopify's dated public record show about running millions of shops on one platform, and what should a merchant that rents a hosted platform do about it?
thesis.claim: Shopify's dated record shows one codebase, deployed as one unit and isolated by shop into database pods, serving millions of shops for a vendor whose revenue moves with the shops' sales and which changes the platform under every merchant on published dates, agent interface included. A renting merchant should plan for those dates (pin connectors to dated API versions, reconcile webhook-fed flows, track extension-point sunsets), not copy pods, shard moves or edge rendering.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that renting a hosted platform hands the architecture to the vendor: the platform's scale and engineering make its integrations reliable and its interfaces stable, so the merchant need only choose apps. A related reading, which the claim also rejects, takes Shopify's lesson for others to be a modular monolith with clean domain boundaries.
thesis.so_what: A merchant on any hosted platform budgets for the vendor's change cadence. Kestrel & Pine takes four lessons: (1) a reconciliation job for every integration (W5); (2) every connector pinned to a dated API version with its support end on the ownership map, after the Deprecated Endpoint's two days of stale stock on bol (W5); (3) nothing customized in checkout that the platform could withdraw, under the app governance rule approved alongside Waypoint; (4) agent readiness through product, availability and order-status APIs and no channel-specific agent build (W8). It rents the pods, renderer and checkout, which is W4.
thesis.how_why: Three quarters of Shopify's FY2025 revenue is merchant solutions that move with merchants' sales, so Shopify protects its own revenue by keeping checkout under its control, changing it on its own schedule while every merchant absorbs the change (the chapter's labeled inference). A single-branch, multi-tenant platform ships every change to every merchant at once, so it keeps checkout upgrade-safe by replacing free-form access with sandboxed extension points and retiring the old ones on announced dates. Its webhook contract promises at-least-once, unordered delivery and deletes a subscription after eight consecutive failures, so a consumer without idempotency and reconciliation loses facts without logging an error. Pods, shard moves and an edge renderer answer the load of millions of shops, which one merchant does not have. The same cadence reached the agent interface: the Storefront MCP tools of May 2025 were replaced by UCP endpoints within a year, so a channel-specific agent build would already have needed rebuilding.

supporting_claims.claim: Shopify's revenue moves with its merchants' sales: in FY2025 three quarters was merchant solutions that the 10-K calls correlated with GMV, two thirds of GMV ran through Shopify Payments, which Shopify resells from licensed processors, and the whole runs as one multi-tenant, single-branch platform, so checkout and payment are its protected paths and every change ships to every merchant at once.

Shopify kept one codebase deployed as one unit; its 2019 to 2024 posts record that domain boundaries did not match how the code works, that durable value came from file ownership and one gate against new base-layer dependencies, and that the one hot path carved out, the Storefront Renderer, was split for measured latency behind a verifier.

The shop is Shopify's sharding key and unit of isolation: shops live in pods with their own datastores and are moved whole, machinery for millions of shops that a merchant does not copy but turns into a question for every vendor: what is your unit of isolation, and can you move or restore my tenant alone?

The platform sets the terms every merchant and integrator works under and changes them on published dates: checkout's free-form access withdrawn from 2023 to 2026 for sandboxed extension points, webhooks that are at-least-once, unordered and deleted after eight consecutive failures, API versions supported for at least twelve months, rate limits per app per store, and an agent interface replaced within a year.

Read with their definitions, Shopify's practices divide into disciplines that transfer to a merchant scaled down (pinning, reconciliation, boundary gates, shadow comparison, load tests on the money paths, isolation questions) and machinery only millions of shops need; Kestrel & Pine takes four lessons that each match a Waypoint decision already made and changes none of its architecture.

The case rests on dated sources of different ages and kinds, kept apart as documented, widely reported or inferred, and the public record stops short of Shopify's current topology, checkout queue, merchant counts, Shop Pay claims and agent-channel terms.

role.contribution: Gives the part a hosted platform's own record, separating the landlord's change cadence and integration contract that a renting merchant must plan for from the machinery only millions of shops need.

flow.rationale: Sections are grouped by subject, each with its own dated evidence, because the reader's question is what the record supports and the age of the evidence differs by subject. 'How to Read This Case' comes first because every later claim is marked by its rules. The business comes before the architecture because it explains the priorities (checkout and payment protected, every change shipped to everyone) the later sections rely on. The monolith precedes the pods because the pods split the data under the one codebase. The parts of the order follow in the order's steps (pages, checkout, payment, stock), then the contract that every app and integration works under, which needs those parts named; peak days follow the rate limits they stress, and the agent surface comes last of the evidence because its argument for adapters needs the cadence the checkout and contract sections have already shown. 'What Transfers' needs all of the evidence, and 'Where the Evidence Stops' bounds it before the take-away. Putting the transfer table first would assert lessons before their evidence; putting the contract before checkout would leave the withdrawn extension points without their timeline.

sections.heading: The Monolith That Stayed: 2019 to 2024

sections.heading: The Shop as the Unit of Isolation: Pods and Moves
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify shards by shop and isolates shops in pods that are moved whole; for a merchant this is not machinery to copy but a question to ask every vendor.

advances_thesis.how: Documents the shop as the unit of isolation and turns it into the merchant's question to vendors.

flow.rationale: 2018 pods, 2021 moves, then the later datastore claims that are often misquoted with the labeled reading, then what the merchant does with it.

transition_in.carries_over: One codebase and one deployment unit.
transition_in.introduces: How the data under that codebase is split and isolated.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify sharded by shop in 2015 when the database could no longer grow on one server, and because one failed shard could then take down the platform it reorganized in 2016 into pods, sets of shops on fully isolated datastores, served by shared workers that talk to one pod at a time (evidence age: eight years).

evidence.what: 'could no longer be scaled by buying a bigger server'; 'A pod consists of a set of shops that live on a fully isolated set of datastores'; 'all shared resources can only ever communicate to a single pod at a time'; a Pod Mover 'in a minute'.
evidence.shows: Isolation by shop was Shopify's answer to shared failure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2021 shard-balancing post shows the mechanism that persisted: shop_id as the sharding key, a routing table from domains to pods, a three-phase move (Ghostferry, a Shopify copying tool, copies rows while the shop stays live) with downtime only at a brief cutover, and placement by measured load and simulation that narrowed the spread between shards from almost four times to about two (evidence age: five years).

evidence.what: 'we can attach a shop_id to all shop-owned tables and have it serve as a sharding key'; Ghostferry copy and replay, cutover lock, routing update; 'The only opportunity for downtime is during the cutover'; 'almost four times' to 'closer to two times'.
evidence.shows: The shop is moved as a whole, with measured placement.

evidence.what: Figure 1: the shop as sharding key and the pod as unit of isolation (routing, containment, moves).
evidence.shows: Shows the three ideas of the section in one picture.

transition_in.introduces: How a shop is moved between them, as documented in 2021.

sections.heading: Storefront Delivery
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify offers three rendering models over one shared cart, checkout and Storefront API, and it polices performance at submission, which for an app-heavy themed store makes the app gate the relevant fact.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the platform setting the terms (shared checkout, performance gates on themes and apps) under which a merchant builds its pages.

flow.rationale: What a rendering model decides, the three models, then the specific performance gates and what they imply.

transition_in.introduces: The first part of the order the merchant sees: the pages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A storefront's rendering model decides which software turns product and cart data into pages and who maintains that software.

Shopify offers three rendering models side by side: themes in its template language Liquid rendered by the Storefront Renderer (modular since Online Store 2.0 in 2021), Hydrogen hosted on Oxygen as its headless toolkit, and any framework against the GraphQL-only Storefront API with three access modes and limits aimed at bots, not buyers.

evidence.what: Online Store 2.0 'fully modular' (Unite, June 2021); Hydrogen 'our modern React-based framework' (2022) and 'Shopify's headless toolkit' (2026); the Storefront API 'is available only in GraphQL'; 'requests from real buyers aren't subject to a fixed request-per-minute limit'; bots limited 'most strictly when unsigned'.
evidence.shows: The three models and what each supplies.

transition_in.introduces: The three models Shopify offers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The performance gates are specific: a minimum Lighthouse score of 60 for Theme Store themes, at most ten points lost per public app, and an admin report that names theme code and apps as causes of slowness; under all three models the cart, checkout and Storefront API are the shared substrate, and the app gate is the fact that matters for Kestrel & Pine's themed storefront with 41 apps.

evidence.what: 'a minimum average Lighthouse performance score of 60'; 'shouldn't reduce Lighthouse performance scores by more than 10 points'; 'some features can slow down your site'.
evidence.source: shopify.dev and Shopify Help Center, accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: The platform polices performance at submission.

evidence.what: > **INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED:** callout (the author's labeled reasoning): a headless storefront still hands off to Shopify's checkout; apps are the usual cause of slow stores and are policed at submission because they cannot be policed after installation; storefront-architecture treats the headless decision.
evidence.shows: Turns the gates into the relevant fact for an app-heavy merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The performance rules that apply across them.

sections.heading: Checkout: Freedom Withdrawn on a Schedule
sections.controlling_idea: From 2021 to 2026 Shopify withdrew free-form checkout customization on published dates and replaced it with sandboxed extension points under hard limits, trading merchant freedom for an upgrade-safe checkout it can change under everyone at once.

advances_thesis.how: The dated reference case for 'the platform will withdraw an extension point'; checkout is where single branch and the revenue model meet.

flow.rationale: The timeline first, then what replaced the freedom with the labeled reading of the arc.

transition_in.carries_over: The pages, which hand off to the shared checkout.
transition_in.introduces: The checkout itself and how its rules changed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checkout is where single branch and the revenue model meet, and its history from June 2021 to August 2026 is a timeline of freedoms withdrawn on published dates, from checkout.liquid to Shopify Scripts and script tags.

evidence.what: Unite 29 June 2021; Winter '23 (9 February 2023); the 13 February 2023 changelog; checkout.liquid stopped 13 August 2024 and 28 August 2025; Scripts editing ends 15 April 2026 and execution 30 June 2026; non-Plus script tags 26 August 2026.
evidence.source: Shopify changelog (2023, 2026), Liquid reference and Help Center (accessed November 2026), Editions pages (2023)
evidence.shows: Each withdrawal was announced and dated.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What replaced the freedom is checkout extensibility: fixed slots for app interface extensions, a branding API, web pixels, and Shopify Functions, backend logic compiled to WebAssembly and invoked by the platform in checkout order under hard limits, with custom Functions and advanced customization only on Plus; read as a whole, the arc traded merchant freedom for an upgrade-safe, PCI-contained checkout Shopify can change under everyone at once, the reference case for planning for withdrawn extension points.

evidence.what: Functions 'allow developers to customize the backend logic of Shopify'; a 256 KiB module, 10 MiB of memory, about 11 million instructions for carts up to 200 lines; 'advanced checkout customization features are available only on the Shopify Plus plan'.
evidence.source: shopify.dev Functions and Function APIs, accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: The replacement is bounded by design.

evidence.what: > **INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED:** callout (the author's labeled reasoning): free-form access withdrawn over three and a half years with dated deadlines, replaced by sandboxed points; the Forked Platform made impossible by design, the Pulled Rug done with notice.
evidence.shows: Names the lesson for the merchant.

evidence.what: Figure 2: an open checkout workshop, then a sealed console with fixed plug-in slots.
evidence.shows: Pictures the before and after of the arc.

transition_in.introduces: What replaced it, and the reading of the whole arc.

sections.heading: Payments: Orchestration, Not a License
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify earns from payments without being a payment institution: it owns the checkout, the Shop Pay wallet and the merchant contract and resells licensed processing.

flow.rationale: What orchestration is, then the terms that show who holds the license, then the wallet the buyer sees in front of it with the labeled reading; the wallet comes after the terms because it is 'included as part of Shopify Payments', and the reading needs both.

advances_thesis.how: Explains how two thirds of GMV runs through Shopify Payments, with Shop Pay in front, while the 10-K names two suppliers.

transition_in.carries_over: The checkout and Shop Pay, included with Shopify Payments.
transition_in.introduces: The payment behind the checkout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Payment orchestration means the platform sends the checkout's payments through separate providers that move the money.

Shopify Payments is the clearest public example of a platform that earns from payments without being a payment institution: its European terms state that no Shopify entity is licensed as a bank or payment institution and name Stripe, PayPal and Adyen as processors.

evidence.what: 'None of the Shopify entities listed above are licensed as a bank, payment institution, or money services business'; Shopify International Limited (Ireland); Stripe Payments Europe, PayPal (Europe), Adyen N.V. for the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany; 41 countries.
evidence.source: Shopify Payments terms (Ireland), processor list, supported countries, accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: The license sits with the processors.

transition_in.introduces: Shopify Payments as the clearest public example.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shop Pay, the accelerated checkout included with Shopify Payments, is the wallet the buyer sees in front of that processing, with vendor conversion claims from an unpublished study and a documented 32% of orders over the 2025 Black Friday weekend; read together, Shopify owns the checkout, the wallet and the merchant contract and resells licensed processing, so whoever owns the checkout owns the payment revenue, licensed or not.

evidence.what: 'an accelerated checkout option', 'included as part of Shopify Payments'; 'as much as 50% better conversion compared to guest checkout' (2023 study, unpublished); 32% of orders, BFCM 2025.
evidence.shows: Separates vendor claims from documented reach, and shows the wallet Shopify owns.

evidence.what: > **INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED:** callout (the author's labeled reasoning): orchestration over licensed processors explains the 10-K's two-supplier concentration risk; commerce-payments owns the mechanics.
evidence.shows: States what the case adds: the business shape of payments.

transition_in.carries_over: The licensed processors behind Shopify Payments.
transition_in.introduces: The wallet the buyer sees in front of them, and the reading of the whole.

sections.heading: Inventory States, Briefly
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify records stock per location in exclusive states, added in steps from 2023 to 2026, but holds no B2B allocation and computes no cross-location available-to-promise, which belongs beside the platform.

advances_thesis.how: Marks where the platform's work ends and the merchant's begins, which is why W1 buys an availability service beside it.

transition_in.introduces: The stock the order draws on.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify's inventory model holds stock per location in exclusive states (available, committed, reserved, damaged, safety stock, quality control, on hand as their sum, incoming apart), added in steps through 5 August 2026, but holds no per-customer B2B allocation and computes no cross-location available-to-promise, which is why Kestrel & Pine's W1 buys an availability service beside the platform.

evidence.what: available 'the inventory that a merchant can sell'; committed 'set aside'; safety_stock 'to help guard against overselling'; on_hand 'the total number of units that are physically at a location'; states added February 2023, August 2023 and 5 August 2026.
evidence.shows: The platform takes on stock states, not allocation or promise.

sections.heading: The Ecosystem: Apps, Scopes, Webhooks and Versions
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify's documentation states the contract every app and integration works under (scopes, webhooks that may be lost, duplicated or reordered, dated API versions and rate limits), and three merchant rules follow from it.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the documented contract behind pinning, idempotency, reconciliation and subscription checks.

flow.rationale: Why apps are part of the merchant's architecture, then the App Store's business and governance, then webhooks, then versions and rate limits with the three rules that follow; webhooks before versions because the first rule (reconcile) is the one the reader needs first.

transition_in.carries_over: The parts of the order the platform runs.
transition_in.introduces: The contract under which apps and integrations reach those parts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Third-party apps add behavior to the shared platform through APIs and notifications, so their permissions, delivery guarantees and upgrade obligations are part of the merchant's architecture.

The App Store is a business (over 21,000 apps, 0% revenue share on the first $1 million and 15% above) and a governance regime: OAuth before anything else, no apps on APIs deprecated within 90 days, three privacy compliance webhooks, and scopes the merchant approves at install.

evidence.what: 'immediately authorize using OAuth before any other steps occur'; 'apps using APIs that will be deprecated within 90 days can't be submitted'; 'your app will be rejected'; 'which store data your app can read and write'; read_orders covering 'orders created within the last 60 days'.
evidence.source: shopify.dev revenue share, app requirements, compliance and access scopes, accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: Access to the merchant's data is gated and scoped by the platform.

transition_in.carries_over: Apps as part of the merchant's architecture.
transition_in.introduces: The App Store's business and governance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Webhooks are the integration contract, and Shopify's own words say delivery is not guaranteed or ordered, duplicates must be ignored by id, reconciliation jobs are expected, and a subscription is deleted after eight consecutive failures over four hours of retries.

evidence.what: 'Webhook delivery isn't always guaranteed'; 'Shopify doesn't guarantee ordering within a topic...'; 'ignore duplicate deliveries using X-Shopify-Webhook-Id'; 'use reconciliation jobs...'; 'it retries 8 times over the next 4 hours'; 'after 8 consecutive failures, the subscription is automatically deleted'; HMAC signature; 13 billion webhooks in 2021.
evidence.source: shopify.dev Webhooks and HTTPS delivery, accessed 2026-11; Shopify Engineering 2022
evidence.shows: The baseline every integrator must assume.

transition_in.introduces: How data changes reach an app: webhooks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: API versions are dated (a new one every three months, each supported at least twelve months, the REST Admin API legacy since October 2024) and rate limits are per app per store by plan; three rules follow: idempotent consumers with reconciliation (W5), a check that the subscription still exists, and rate limits treated as a tenancy budget on a peak day.

evidence.what: 'Shopify releases a new API version every three months', 'supported for a minimum of 12 months', 'falls forward'; 'a legacy API as of October 1, 2024'; 100, 1,000 and 2,000 points a second; 'Shopify might temporarily reduce API rate limits to protect platform stability'.
evidence.source: shopify.dev versioning and rate limits, accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: Change and capacity are dated and bounded.

evidence.what: Figure 3: the documented integration contract (scopes, rate limits, at-least-once unordered webhooks, reconciliation, dated versions).
evidence.shows: Puts the whole contract in one view.

evidence.what: > **INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED:** callout (the author's labeled reasoning): idempotency and reconciliation are W5 in Shopify's own words; a connector down for five hours on a Friday night has no subscription on Saturday morning; a polling connector can starve another app.
evidence.shows: Turns the contract into three merchant rules.

transition_in.introduces: Versions and rate limits, and the rules that follow from the whole contract.

sections.heading: Peak Days With Definitions
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify's Black Friday figures are useful only with their caveats, and its documented preparation, scaled down, gives a merchant a program for its own connectors, ERP and WMS.

advances_thesis.how: Separates the transferable peak practices from figures and machinery at Shopify's scale.

transition_in.carries_over: Rate limits as a peak-day constraint.
transition_in.introduces: Shopify's own peak days and how it prepares for them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify's Black Friday-Cyber Monday figures for 2023 to 2025 are unaudited, not directly comparable across years and report no order count, and must be read with those caveats.

evidence.what: BFCM 2023-2025: sales $9.3, $11.5 and $14.6 billion; peak sales per minute $4.2, $4.6 and $5.1 million; peak load; database queries and writes; Shop Pay; merchants with their best day.
evidence.source: Shopify announcements of 28 November 2023, 2 December 2024 and 2 December 2025
evidence.shows: The scale of the platform's peak and how the definitions change.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify's preparation is documented for 2023 (full-scale tests with part of the traffic bypassing the CDN and an abort switch) and 2025 (capacity planning from March, game days on the money paths, five scale tests that exposed errors and rate-limit paths), with the checkout queue documented only in 2018; scaled down, the transferable practices are testing at forecast load with caches bypassed, rehearsing failure on the money paths and decoupling payment from order creation.

evidence.what: 'full-scale approach'; 'bypass the CDN for a portion of the traffic'; 'started in March with capacity planning'; 'critical journeys'; '146 million requests per minute and 80,000+ checkouts per minute'; 'core operations threw errors and checkout queues backed up'; 2018: 'processing payments at checkout happens separately from creating orders'.
evidence.shows: The preparation program and its findings, dated.

evidence.what: > **INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED:** callout (the author's labeled reasoning): edge requests about four times app-server requests; a platform peak-to-average ratio of about two against a single merchant's 41-times spike; the practices scaled down to connectors, ERP and WMS.
evidence.shows: Explains why the platform's peak is not the merchant's and what transfers.

transition_in.carries_over: The peak figures and their caveats.
transition_in.introduces: How Shopify prepares for them and what that means for a merchant.

sections.heading: AI and the Agent Surface: Rebuilt Within a Year
sections.controlling_idea: Shopify's admin assistant and its agent-facing interfaces are different uses; the agent interface was replaced within a year, and no EU buyer market is in scope.

advances_thesis.how: The agent interface is the newest example of the platform changing under every merchant on published dates.

flow.rationale: Sidekick (2023-2026), then the agent interface in date order, then its geography, which is what a European merchant needs and closes the section.

transition_in.carries_over: The integration contract and peak days.
transition_in.introduces: The newest surface on the platform: AI.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify's AI for merchants and its interfaces for outside agents are different uses with different permissions; Sidekick, the admin assistant announced in 2023, runs reports and proposes changes with the merchant's approval, and its general-availability date and growth figure are unverified or vendor claims.

evidence.what: Sidekick announced July 2023; 21 May 2025 capabilities 'with the merchant's approval'; help page (accessed November 2026); 4.2-times growth in daily sessions (Fall 2026 edition, vendor figure).
evidence.source: Shopify Summer '25, Sidekick help, Fall '26 Edition
evidence.shows: The assistant proposes; the merchant approves.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The agent-facing side is the clearest dated example of protocol churn: the Storefront MCP server of May 2025, Agentic Storefronts for every merchant in December 2025, the Universal Commerce Protocol and Agentic plan in January 2026, and by November 2026 the MCP catalog and cart tools removed in favor of UCP endpoints with agent profiles and trust tiers.

evidence.what: 'available to every merchant' (10 December 2025); 'no monthly fee', 'from 1.9% + €0.25' (11 January 2026); 'were removed', UCP 'now provides these capabilities'; 'requires authenticated or signed requests'; 'higher trust tiers unlock broader access, including direct checkout completion'; caching at most fifteen minutes; 'endpoint URLs might change'.
evidence.source: shopify.dev agents, Catalog, Storefront MCP; Shopify news 2025-2026
evidence.shows: The interface changed within a year, on dates.

transition_in.introduces: The interfaces for outside agents, which can buy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The geography is the fact a European merchant needs: the ChatGPT channel requires selling to US customers, Google's direct checkout serves only the US, Canada and Australia, and no EU buyer market is in scope on any page read at the cut-off, which makes a platform that replaced its agent interface within a year the strongest argument for adapters over one internal API.

evidence.what: 'your store must sell to customers in the United States'; OpenAI's March 2026 retreat from in-chat checkout; Google channel limits.
evidence.source: Shopify Help Center agentic storefronts, accessed 2026-11; Modern Retail 2026

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The business, the architecture, the checkout timeline, the integration contract and the agent surface give one answer to the opening question: the landlord takes on the machinery (one codebase, pods, the renderer, the checkout and its peak) and changes the platform under everyone on dates it publishes, while the merchant keeps the joins (every connector pinned, every webhook-fed flow reconciled, every extension point's sunset tracked).
conclusion.so_what: A merchant on any hosted platform budgets for the vendor's change cadence as maintenance work with owners and dates, and asks its vendors for their unit of isolation and their contract terms, instead of copying the vendor's machinery or assuming the vendor's scale makes its integrations reliable.

callback.to: The opening question: which work the platform takes on and which work the merchant's team still operates.
callback.how: p44 answers it with the record the chapter has read: the machinery is the landlord's, the joins and the calendar are the merchant's.

takeaway.content: Inventory every app, connector and extension point with its API version, support end and owner; reconcile every webhook-fed flow and check that its subscription still exists; keep custom behavior out of the checkout; ask each vendor for its unit of isolation.
